items.title: [ArchDaily] In the Wake of the 2024 Floods in Southern Brazil: Restore the Past or Rethink the Future?
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

In May 2024, the floods that hit Rio Grande do Sul exposed a contradiction common to contemporary cities. Many were built alongside rivers and shaped by their presence, yet spent decades trying to control water without incorporating its dynamics into urban planning. Extreme weather events will intensify that vulnerability. More than two years later, reconstruction in the Brazilian state has progressed, infrastructure has been restored, and new protection strategies are taking shape. But are these cities rebuilding their relationship with water, or only restoring the systems that failed?

items.content_html:

Scientists have created a miniature universe in the laboratory that could help answer one of the biggest mysteries in physics: What is time, and where does it come from? Using 24,000 ultracold atoms, a University of Birmingham researcher built an isolated quantum system that repeatedly expands and contracts, mimicking the Big Bang and a possible Big Crunch. Remarkably, the experiment showed that time could emerge from changes happening inside the system, without relying on an external clock.

items.title: [Fast Company] Why driverless trucks won’t be taking over highways just yet
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Driverless trucks with artificial intelligence on board could dramatically change the landscape of freight shipping. A few companies have begun testing early models on some limited routes in Texas and California. Simulations of automated fleets show the potential benefits of the technology: The vehicles could improve safety, enhance fuel economy, and lessen transit times.

Truck makers and operators still have to solve some major issues, however, including how automated trucks will operate in variable weather and road conditions, and whether drivers should still be inside big rigs.

I am an engineer who studies human factors and transportation safety, and in my view, it is likely that automated trucks and human drivers will be working together for quite some time.

Benefits of automation

Fully automated trucks, which can drive on an interstate highway in good weather without human intervention, use a combination of AI, machine learning, computer vision, pattern recognition, and adaptive decision-making. Torc, one company developing these vehicles, uses AI to combine data from multiple sensors and generate models that predict truck performance.

Data taken from modern big rigs that are equipped with certain technology such as automatic emergency braking and lane-keeping assistance systems indicate that fully automated, driverless trucks could reduce the number and severity of crashes. They could also save fuel and therefore cost by optimizing acceleration and braking, and by running multiple vehicles in a close-knit convoy or platoon. Driverless trucks could reduce parking needs as well as emissions from idling because they could run almost 24 hours a day and would not need to idle when they do park, which is common for regular rigs at truck stops.

Finally, automated trucks could help ease the ongoing driver shortage. Ironically, automation could make driving less stressful and less physically demanding, improving job satisfaction among drivers.

Weather and work zones are hard to navigate

The main reason automated trucks are not common today is that they have difficulty operating in variable weather, under changing roadway conditions, and alongside unpredictable drivers.

Automated trucks require sensors, radars, and cameras that gather information about the environment around them to make decisions. However, snow and rain remain a problem for all automated vehicles, including cars, because they prevent the technology from “seeing” the roadway. Driverless taxi company Waymo, for example, operates driverless cars only in areas that get no snow.

Furthermore, any stretch of road where there may not be a predictable, clear surface and prevalent lines is difficult to handle. Imagine a construction zone with orange cones, narrow lanes, and missing lane lines. Driverless car companies still try to avoid these areas. And, oddly, some research shows that automobile drivers tend to crash into driverless cars at a higher rate than they do cars piloted by people.

Given those challenges, companies are testing automated trucks on roads that lack complications.

For example, autonomous truck maker Aurora is operating large freight trucks on I-45, a relatively flat and straight highway between Dallas and Houston. Rival Kodiak’s robotrucks are delivering sand to industrial sites in Texas over roads few people use. Few if any automated trucks are being tested in chaotic urban environments, given the pedestrians, bicyclists, traffic lights, and elements of city traffic.

Driverless trucks are operating on some roads in Texas.

Some companies that were developing automated trucks have scaled back ambitions, changed direction, or exited the market.

In 2023, Embark, TuSimple, and Locomotion closed down. Waymo began to focus solely on cars. Other companies narrowed their focus to trucks that would operate only along a few dedicated routes between two large cities or manufacturing sites.

Drivers and trucks that work together

In my view, for years to come, automated trucks with AI-based controls will still require a driver.

The best technology will support a symbiosis between human and machine, where the person and the truck each do what they do best. A human would likely drive the truck across the “first mile”—the uncertain and crowded warehouse grounds and local streets to a highway. The driver would then stop using the steering wheel, gas pedal, and brake and let automation take over. The human would take back control during the “last mile” to the truck’s final destination.

Research my colleagues and I conducted shows that human-machine interfaces that communicate between drivers and autonomous vehicles will be key. For example, a screen or head-up display inside the cab would tell the driver how the technology is doing. Verbal messages or a vibrating seat could signal that the automation cannot handle a developing situation, and the driver would take over.

Developers will have to be aware of possible biases. So-called automation bias could lead to a driver who trusts and relies on the truck’s decision-making so much that they defer to it. Algorithmic bias could cause truck sensors to recognize certain groups of people on the road more than others, such as only detecting pedestrians of a certain size or shape.

The long-term vision is to have no driver, in part to lower costs. But driverless trucks do not seem to me to be practical on a large scale in the near future. It is more realistic to envision the driver and the automated truck as a team. Vehicle manufacturers, technology developers, regulators, and drivers will need to work together to realize the benefits.

🎨 ✏️

Youth-led demonstrations over living costs, education, housing and public services drew crowds across Europe on Saturday, with violence breaking out after rallies in several German cities. Organizers of Germany’s “Gen Z regelt” movement estimated 120,000 participants across more than 30 cities. Most marches were peaceful, but looting, fires and clashes with police followed rallies in Frankfurt, Berlin, Cologne and Hamburg. In Frankfurt, authorities reported at least 54 arrests and more than 100 injured police officers. France’s third consecutive weekend of protests drew an estimated 320,000 people, including 70,000 in Paris, according to the Interior Ministry; police made 779 arrests nationwide. Demonstrations also took place in Portugal, where police cleared a tent camp in Lisbon after a housing protest, and in Zurich, where police said rioters set vehicles and barricades alight. Participants in Germany also opposed spending cuts and plans to revive compulsory military service. Organizers rejected violence, while German officials blamed extremist groups and called for penalties against those involved. Gen Z regelt has called for another demonstration on Nov. 14; a separate Europe-wide protest is planned for Nov. 20.

items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Governments at the U.N. biodiversity summit, COP17, agreed to accelerate efforts to cut subsidies that damage nature, including support for fossil fuels, but left unresolved how to fund conservation. Nearly 200 countries adopted the Yerevan Pathway in Armenia after the first review found the world off track on almost all biodiversity goals for 2030. The agreement calls for countries to revise their biodiversity plans to address gaps in marine, coastal and inland-water protection and accelerate efforts to reduce harmful incentives by at least $500 billion a year by 2030. Developed countries missed a commitment to provide at least $20 billion annually for nature by 2025, while environmental funding is projected to fall 27% over 2026-30, Carbon Brief reported. Organizers said governments, philanthropies and investors announced more than $1.8 billion in nature finance at the summit, compared with the framework’s goal of mobilizing $200 billion a year by 2030. Countries invited non-donor states to express interest in joining the donor list, but deferred a decision on the structure of a permanent post-2030 financing mechanism until COP18 in Quito in 2028. The U.N. climate conference COP31 begins in Antalya, Türkiye, on Nov. 9.

items.title: [Fast Company] Hackers hijacked a Claude Code extension, exposing yet another new AI security risk
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

The world can feel particularly unsafe these days, with AI agents running rampant within private networks and billions of dollars disappearing from crypto wallets in less time than it takes to watch a sitcom episode.

But while the world was watching Binance’s massive crypto heist, another potentially consequential security breach was unfolding largely under the radar.

For roughly 11 hours, a malicious version of Anthropic’s Claude Code extension was available on Cursor’s VS Code extension marketplace. The extension—which allows developers to use Anthropic’s AI coding assistant within Cursor to write, edit, and debug software—had been tampered with to collect information about users’ computers and attempt to install a persistent backdoor. That backdoor used Secure Shell (SSH), a tool for remotely accessing computers, and could potentially have allowed hackers to access victims’ machines even after the extension was removed.

Cursor disclosed the breach in a blog post, saying it removed the compromised extension as soon as it discovered the problem. The company also emphasized that the mechanism intended to give hackers remote access was unlikely to have worked in many cases because of flaws in its code. Anthropic, meanwhile, said in a statement that the incident “only impacts Cursor users” and was unrelated to Anthropic’s own systems.

According to Cursor’s security notice, the malicious extension was designed to leave behind scripts that would attempt to reconnect to the hackers’ server every minute, even after the extension had been removed. Cursor says it has since worked with the server’s hosting provider to take the server offline and to temporarily shut down and rebuild its extension marketplace. The company found no evidence that other extensions were compromised. Still, it is urging anyone who installed the affected version on October 29 to check their computers for signs of infection, remove any unauthorized access, and consider changing potentially compromised credentials.

The hackers’ identities remain unknown, but security experts say the incident illustrates an increasingly troubling risk as AI coding tools become embedded in developers’ workflows.

“The scenario of Claude sending out poisoned agents everywhere makes me even more worried than I already was,” says Eerke Boiten, a professor of cybersecurity at De Montfort University in England.

Gwen van der Velden, a professor of education at the University of Warwick who’s working on a program to help rebuild Ukraine, says the choice of the Claude Code extension is particularly “interesting” given the potential for such tools to be exploited in hybrid warfare.

“We know from the Russian side, it is of great interest to them,” she says. “If you were to go for hybrid warfare, where you use this kind of technology, then actually getting 5,000 bits of malware reproducing itself through AI agents is a powerful thing.”

The broader concern isn’t simply that a malicious extension could compromise individual computers. It’s that the growing ecosystem of AI coding assistants and their associated tools is creating new pathways into sensitive systems.

“This is a classic example of how everyone has been focussing on LLMs attacking other systems, yet forgetting about the fact that LLMs and their associated tools are increasing the attack surface across some very sensitive IT estates,” says Alan Woodward, a professor of cybersecurity at the University of Surrey.

And even a relatively limited breach could carry outsized consequences when the targets are software developers with access to sensitive code and infrastructure.

“While 5,000 users might sound relatively small, these are developers who have access to highly sensitive systems and source code, so the potential impact will be far greater than the numbers suggest,” says Jake Moore, a threat adviser with the global cybersecurity firm ESET. “Software extensions have eased their way into many people’s workflows, but the concern is how easily trusted software extensions can become a vehicle for malicious code.”

items.title: [zmescience.com] Protein evidence identifies Chinese fossils as Denisovans, revealing likely facial traits
items.content_html:
🎨 ✏️

Researchers have identified human fossils from Xujiayao in northern China as Denisovans using ancient proteins, then compared their bones with other remains to infer the group’s likely appearance. The fossils suggest Denisovans had low, backward-sloping foreheads, heavy brow ridges and broad, relatively flat faces, with features distinct from those of Neanderthals. The team recovered a Denisovan-linked collagen variant from two fossils with no surviving DNA. The Xujiayao collection includes 20 specimens excavated decades ago. The researchers argue that some Chinese fossils previously assigned to separate human groups may instead represent variation within the Denisovan lineage. That classification remains uncertain for specimens identified only by resemblance, and researchers say additional samples would help test it.

items.content_html:

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law on Oct. 28 barring AI chatbot companies from offering users under 18 unsafe features, including pretending to be human, claiming a relationship with a child, encouraging self-harm or providing sexually explicit material. The law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027, and requires companies to verify users’ ages using more than one method, including an option that does not rely solely on government ID, then delete the age-verification data. The New York attorney general can seek penalties of up to $25,000 per violation, damages and orders to destroy unlawfully collected data or models trained on it. The office must also provide a public complaint portal. Hochul cited the case of Adam Raine, a California teenager who died by suicide after prolonged chatbot use, saying the chatbot had discussed self-harm with him. States have enacted AI rules while Congress has not adopted comprehensive federal standards. New York’s law takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.

🎨 ✏️

A study of more than 100,000 UK Biobank participants found that a 1972 British law requiring teenagers to stay in school until 16 was associated with fewer diagnoses of Alzheimer’s disease and related dementias nearly 50 years later. Using the reform’s September 1, 1957, birth-date cutoff, researchers compared people subject to different school-leaving rules and reported a 0.88% reduction in dementia incidence among those affected. Researchers also found the reduction among participants with high genetic susceptibility. They cautioned that dementia was uncommon in this cohort, whose diagnoses were tracked only through age 65, making the estimate imprecise. Continued follow-up will help determine whether the difference persists as participants age.

Reform reach: The change increased the share of students who remained in school until at least age 16 by 14 percentage points (phys.org, abril.com.br, welltica.dk).
